Abstract
The increasing number of medical devices in the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) en­
vironment has raised significant cybersecurity concerns. These devices often have weak 
security features, poor design, and insufficient authentication protocols, making them vul­
nerable to cyberattacks and intrusions. To mitigate these threats, robust security measures 
are essential. This includes implementing strong security protocols, ensuring continuous 
security monitoring, enforcing regular updates, and maintaining a constant response plan. 
Additionally, designing an effective Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is crucial to safe­
guard patient data and devices. This paper systematically studies the current state of the 
literature and the essential methods for intrusion detection in the IoMT. Employing a se­
lection process, the paper identifies 28 critical studies published between 2018 and April 
2024. The intrusion detection mechanisms in the IoMT are divided into five categories: 
IDS based on artificial intelligence models, datasets used in IoMT for IDS, fundamental 
security requirements, intrusion detection processes, and evaluation metrics. This paper 
dissects the various mechanisms within each category in a meticulous and comprehensive 
analysis. Finally, the paper examines the challenges and open issues in developing IDSs 
in IoMT. By offering a roadmap for researchers to enhance IDSs in the IoMT, this paper 
has the potential to significantly impact the fields of computer engineering, cybersecurity, 
and healthcare, thereby contributing to the advancement of these crucial fields.

1  Introduction
The traditional health and medical systems cannot respond quickly, handle variations of 
illnesses and treatments, and meet the needs of patients in real-time due to the increasing 
number of patients and limited resources (Yaacoub et al. 2020). For this reason, using the 
Internet of Things (IoT) in medicine and health can overcome the mentioned problems, and 
patients and health workers can easily connect to medical devices based on IoT through 
Internet services(Gharehchopogh et al. 2023a). The integration of the IoT with medical 
devices is called the IoMT or the Internet of Health Things (IoHT) (Chaganti et al. 2022). 
Other names and terms used in articles and research instead of IoMT are Internet of Things 
Health, Smart Health, Health 4.0, and Internet of Things-Health (Hernandez-Jaimes et al. 
2023). The IoMT is a heterogeneous, distributed, and scalable network of medical and wear­
able devices connected to the internet, applications, hardware, and software infrastructure 
(Pradyumna et al. 2024). This network supports information technology systems in health­
care. IoMT also facilitates connections between health services through network and online 
technologies (Khan et al. 2023). IoMT devices perform real-time data collection and analy­
sis, continuously monitoring patients from afar, allowing early detection, specialized care, 
and intervention in chronic conditions. Also, it allows for personalized treatment plans, 
more accurate disease management, reduced hospital readmissions, and rapid alert systems. 
According to Frost and Sullivan, the global IoMT market has an annual growth rate of 
$72.02 billion and $22.5 billion in 2016 and 2021, respectively, and nearly 30 billion IoMT 
devices have been used in 2021 (Kumar et al. 2021; Abdulkareem and Sani 2023). In the 
coming years, IoMT is anticipated to capture the lion's share of the IoT market, driven by 
the growing people's awareness and demand for IoMT devices and advancements in new 
technologies. It will constitute approximately 30% of the IoT devices market (Kakhi et 
al. 2022). Recent research has shown that the IoMT market is expected to hit a stagger­
ing $135.87 billion by 2025, which indicates that IoMT has created a great revolution in 
medical and health systems (Chaganti et al. 2022; Kakhi et al. 2022; Ravi et al. 2023). In 
2022, the market was valued at approximately USD 48.7 billion, and it is projected to reach 
an estimated USD 370.9 billion by 2032, growing at a Compound Annual Growth Rate 
(CAGR) of 23.15% (Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) Market CAGR Of 23.15%, 2023). 
However, different reports suggest varying growth rates, with some predicting a CAGR 
of 20.4% from 2023 to 2030 and a projected market size of USD 668.07 billion by 2030 
(Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) Market Size Report 2030, 2023). Additionally, an even 
higher forecast suggests growth from USD 60.03 billion in 2024 to USD 814.28 billion by 
2032, reflecting a CAGR of 38.5% (Internet of Medical Things [IoMT] Market Size and 
Growth, 2032, 2024). These figures highlight the substantial potential for growth in the 
IoMT market over the coming years. Figure 1 shows the size of the IoMT market between 
2022 and 2032 (Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) Market CAGR Of 23.15%, 2023).
IoMT plays a vital role in increasing the quality of life, accuracy, reliability, efficiency, 
and effectiveness of health systems, reducing costs, saving hospital resources, improving 
healthcare operations, and reducing medical errors, disease control, failure reduction, moni­
toring patients in real-time and continuously from a distance by a doctor, early diagnosis of 
diseases in the initial stages, increasing the efficiency of treatment and access to health care 
in rural areas that lack medical infrastructure (Si-Ahmed et al. 2023; Hireche et al. 2022).

1.1  IoMT architecture
IoMT architecture has the data collection layer (perception layer), the network layer (data 
management), and the application layer (medical service) (Aman et al. 2021). Figure 2 
shows the structure of IoMT architecture. The data collection layer comprises medical 
devices and sensors connected to patients and stimuli. Sensors such as temperature sensors, 
biological sensors, pulse and heart rate detectors, ECG devices, blood pressure devices, 
breathing rate monitoring devices, etc., reside in this layer. They are responsible for gath­
ering sensitive and real-time patient data and transmitting it to the network layer. Due to 
energy constraints in IoMT devices, short-range communication technologies, including 
Bluetooth, Near-Field Communication (NFC), and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID), 
are employed for data transmission. This layer faces some attacks, including physical and 
device manipulation, routing, sensor tracking, impersonating, tampering, jamming, RFID 
cloning, and malicious code injection attacks (Khatun et al. 2023). The limited computing 
and storage capacity of IoMT devices hinders their ability to process and analyze data. In 
rare cases, they are only able to perform the preprocessing stage. The network layer trans­
fers the collected data (network traffic data and patient biometric data) to the cloud using 
communication technologies such as Wi-Fi and communication protocols such as MQTT 
and AMQP. After performing the necessary processing and analysis, this layer sends the 
results to the third layer, i.e., the application layer, for storage and visualization. Long-
range network technologies, such as GSM, Wi-Fi, GPRS, etc., transfer information to the 
third layer. Some of the attacks that this layer faces are eavesdropping, replay, fraudulent, 
signaling, Denial of Service (DoS), wormhole, Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS), syn­
chronization, Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), Sibyl, network injection, and personal attacks 
(Hernandez-Jaimes et al. 2023). The application layer is also responsible for data analysis, 
monitoring, preparing reports, and sending necessary notifications to patients and doctors 
for action and decision-making (Chaganti et al. 2022; Mamdouh et al. 2021). This layer 
facilitates the secure health information exchange between doctors and patients, allowing 
on-demand access and data upload/download. It also faces data leakage, DoS, SQL injec­
tion, malware, phishing, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks, brute force, location threats, 
warnings, and ransomware attacks.
Various architectures have been proposed for IOMT in different articles, with the primary 
distinction lying in the number of layers and the tasks assigned to each layer. In (Rani et al. 
2023), the IOMT architecture comprises four layers: the sensor layer, the gateway layer, the 
cloud layer, and the visualization layer. The sensor layer is responsible for data collection, 
the gateway layer handles data transmission, the cloud layer is tasked with data analysis 
and storage, and the visualization layer is accountable for medical data presentation. In 
(Hernandez-Jaimes et al. 2023), the IoMT architecture comprises four layers: the perception 
layer, network layer, transport layer, and application layer. The perception layer consists of 
medical devices and sensors for medical data gathering. The network layer connected all 
IoMT components through wireless, wired, and middleware technologies. The transport 
layer acts as a data highway, ensuring the secure and complete transfer of collected physi­

1.2  Intrusion detection system
An IDS continuously and autonomously monitors network activities and sends alerts to net­
work administrators when it detects and identifies suspicious or malicious activity (Naseri 
and Gharehchopogh 2022; Samadi Bonab et al. 2020). An IDS consists of three main com­
ponents: the monitoring/information source, the detection/analysis engine, and the response. 
The monitoring component continuously analyzes the network traffic flow, system events, 
and behavior. The detection/analysis engine component identifies any suspicious activity 
and relays it to the response component. The response component notifies the network man­
ager or initiates an alarm (Rbah et al. 2022). Responses can be active (e.g., disconnecting a 
device) or passive (e.g., sending a warning)). Medical systems face two main attack types: 
external and remote attacks that attackers from outside the network carry out and internal 
attacks perpetrated by doctors or staff who access patient data for unauthorized purposes. 
The performance of an IDS is different from other security methods, such as firewalls or 
antiviruses. An IDS monitors network traffic and analyzes events to uncover suspicious

1.2.1  Taxonomies of IDSs in IoMT
IoMT devices are susceptible to various attacks and unauthorized access and lack protocols, 
security controls, standards, and robust authentication mechanisms (Al-Hawawreh and Hos­
sain 2023). Attacks in the IoMT environment can be classified from different perspectives. 
Kumar et al. (2021) classified attacks into four types: attacks on IoMT physical devices 
and sensors, attacks between communication media, attacks against healthcare providers, 
and attacks on patients. Cyberattacks, security breaches, privacy concerns, and intrusion 
detection are the most critical challenges in IoMT. Deviating consequences can occur with­
out an efficient, scalable, and distributed system to deal with these threats. These include 
loss of data confidentiality, integrity, and availability, as well as data transmission delays, 
device failures, and device malfunctions, all of which can have irreparable consequences 
for patients (Mamdouh et al. 2021). In Yaacoub et al. (2020), the existing methods for main­
taining security and privacy in IoMT were divided into encryption and non-encryption. It is 
challenging to implement encryption solutions in IoMT devices. For this purpose, studies 
have shown that to overcome existing problems, IDSs have better performance. There is a 
critical need for an effective and reliable IDS with minimal FAR, high accuracy, and fast 
attack detection capabilities. This IDS should continuously monitor the network, identify 
malicious activity and suspicious behavior, and promptly issue necessary warnings. IDSs 
can be categorized based on various criteria. Figure 3 presents a combined classification 
for IDSs, drawing upon various classification schemes presented in prior works, includ­
ing (Yaacoub et al. 2020; Dutta and Granjal 2020; Mishra and Pandya 2021). IDSs play a 
critical role in securing the healthcare industry. Each type of IDS performs different tasks 
according to its nature, such as detecting known threats in IoMT devices and detecting 
abnormal behaviors in patient data. IDS architectures can implement IDS at various levels, 
from individual devices to wide hospital networks. Devices in IoMT have challenges such 
as the limitation of computing resources and energy, the need for real-time responsiveness, 
and maintaining a balance between security and efficiency, highlighting the importance of 
choosing and intelligently combining these methods. ML and AI techniques in IDSs allow 
for better adaptability to emerging threats and reduce FAR. A deep understanding of the 
relationship between the types of IDSs provides the possibility of designing more effective

Online IDS continuously monitors data streams to identify intrusions in real time and 
acts as the first line of defense. Online IDS analyzes network traffic, identifies suspicious 
activities and unusual patterns, and prevents the spread of malware to other devices in 
IoMT environments. Offline IDS analyzes historical data stored in persistent sources like 
databases to uncover intrusion patterns. In these systems, it is possible to perform detailed 
data analysis, identify more complex patterns and hidden threats that cannot be detected by 
online methods, and produce detailed reports of threats and vulnerabilities. These systems 
may be associated with delays and damage and endangering patients' lives. Due to the time-
sensitive nature of intrusion detection, online IDSs are prioritized, while offline IDSs play 
a supporting role. Additionally, online systems can share information with offline systems, 
enriching historical data and increasing the effectiveness of offline (Zipperle et al. 2022). In 
the category of IDS based on behavior and reaction, active IDS take the necessary action to 
deal with an alarm (Thakkar and Lohiya 2022). Active IDS react quickly to threats detected 
in critical devices, such as devices connected to patients, and disconnect suspicious con­
nections to prevent the spread of infection in the IoMT network. Still, passive IDS do not 
take the required action and only activate reports or warnings (Mishra and Pandya 2021). 
Passive IDS monitors the network traffic of medical devices without interfering with their 
operation, gathers information to analyze traffic patterns, and prevents attacks in the IoMT 
environment.
IDS are divided into seven subcategories: rule-based, anomaly-based, signature-based, 
specifications-based, reputation-based, Stateful Protocol Analysis (SPA)-based, and hybrid 
IDS. Rule-based IDSs, with their adaptability, can accurately identify existing attack pat­
terns and cannot identify unknown, undefined, and new attacks. Rule-based IDS defines 
specific rules for the permitted behaviors of various medical devices and detects deviations 
from standard protocols in IoMT communications. This IDS must continuously update the 
rules based on protocol changes and new devices. Anomaly-based IDSs use AI or statistical 
algorithms to model normal user behavior. These IDSs detect abnormal behaviors in data 
transmission patterns from medical devices. Anomaly-based IDS, unlike rules-based IDS, 
can identify unknown, zero-day, and existing types of attacks. Anomaly-based IDS has a 
higher FAR and may lead to a reduction of false alarms caused by natural changes in the 
condition of patients (Binbusayyis and Vaiyapuri 2021). Additionally, given the constrained 
computing resources and the vast number of connected devices, anomaly-based IDS proves 
to be inefficient for IoMT scenarios (Yaacoub et al. 2020). For this reason, rule-based IDS is 
preferred over anomaly-based IDS (Ravi et al. 2023). Signature-based (misuse-based) and 
specification-based IDS require lower overhead than anomaly-based methods. In signature-
based IDS, the incoming network traffic patterns are compared with patterns related to intru­
sions that have already been stored in the related database (Ahmad et al. 2023). In case of 
a mismatch, a necessary warning is issued. As a result, they are not successful in detecting 
zero-day attacks and intrusion detection in the IoMT network, and the database related to 
predefined attacks must be updated continuously. Signature-based IDS, with its precision, 
uses methods such as pattern mapping and state mapping to detect intrusion (Ksibi et al. 
2023). Signature-based IDS has a lower FAR than anomaly-based IDS, but it has disadvan­
tages, such as it can detect fewer attacks and is difficult to maintain. Specifications-based

and low false positives. The effectiveness of this IDS depends on the quality and timeli­
ness of the reputation data, and the database related to pre-defined attacks must be updated 
continuously. Also, these IDS are not successful in detecting zero-day attacks and intru­
sion detection in the IoMT network (Verma and Chandra 2023). SPA-based IDS analyzes, 
monitors, and tracks states, transport, application, and context of network protocols across 
time to identify abnormal behavior or security risks. Unlike signature-based IDS, which 
detect attacks by matching patterns to known signatures, SPA-based IDS focuses on the 
state and behavior of network protocols, considering their context and expected sequences 
of interactions. SPA-based IDS excels in detecting protocol-specific anomalies with low 
false positives, but the anomaly detection IDS offers broader threat detection capabilities 
and can identify unknown threats at the cost of higher false positives and resource require­
ments (Arnaboldi and Morisset 2021). In the category network structure/placement strate­
gies, IDSs are divided into six sub-categories: centralized, distributed, mobile, hierarchical, 
cooperative, and hybrid. Centralized IDS perform data analysis at specific and designated 
points within a network.
Typically, the IDS is deployed on a border router or a cluster head, which functions as a 
central collection point. This router or head forwards traffic data from individual nodes to 
the core IDS. The core IDS then examines the combined traffic stream for signs of intru­
sion attempts. This method has scalability issues and is effective for smaller networks. A 
distributed IDS consists of many IDSs connected to a central server or each other over an 
extensive network and is responsible for network tracking and attack investigation. A decen­
tralized IDS system offers several advantages: scalability, privacy preservation, real-time 
detection, and resilience (Heidari and Jabraeil Jamali 2023; Tariq et al. 2024). The hybrid 
IDS is a hybrid strategy that avoids the drawbacks of these approaches while utilizing their 
advantages. Cooperative IDS are scalable and adaptable IDS for identifying multi-stage 
and distributed attacks and contextual and collaborative analysis. Cooperative IDS con­
sists of several IDSs that work together and share information within a single network or 
between multiple networks to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of detecting threats. 
This IDS improved detection accuracy and decreased false positives (Bansal and Singhrova 
2024). A hierarchical IDS is a scalable multi-tiered architecture (consisting of local agents, 
intermediate nodes, and a central management system) to monitor and analyze network traf­
fic and identify suspicious activities and potential intrusions in a network or system. This 
IDS uses a hierarchical structure to improve detection accuracy and scalability and reduce 
the processing load (Verkerken et al. 2023). Mobile IDS are responsible for real-time and 
constant monitoring, detecting, and protecting mobile devices and dynamic environments 
from security threats, anomalies, and malicious activities. Mobile IDS detects and responds 
to malicious activities by analyzing user behavior, network traffic, application, and sys­
tem integrity. Resource constraints, operating system diversity, high mobility, user privacy, 
and ever-increasing complexity of security threats are some challenges encountered during 
MIDS implementation (Ribeiro et al. 2018; Kaur et al. 2018).

In the classification of IDS based on data source/architecture, IDS are divided into three

because one IDS is required for each host (Mishra and Pandya 2021; Lin et al. 2023). Host-
based IDSs cannot provide a complete IDS due to the dynamic, varied, and changing nature 
of attacks and are slow and unable to detect external attacks. Network-based IDSs monitor 
the network traffic of multiple IoMT devices to detect any malicious activity (Yaacoub et al. 
2020). Network-based IDSs have an excellent ability to detect external intrusions, but they 
have much traffic (Mishra and Pandya 2021). In most IoMT devices, because these devices 
have tiny memory, the use of network-based IDS is preferred to host-based IDS, especially 
in the place of IoMT gateways (Ravi et al. 2023). A hybrid IDS combines the strengths and 
capabilities of host-based and network-based IDS. It is more secure and compatible because 
it uses the features of these two IDS. In the classification of IDS based on AI, IDS are 
divided into three categories: ML-based IDS, DL-based IDS, and ensemble-based IDS. In 
some research, researchers have used data-mining methods to detect attacks and intrusions 
in IoMT (Swarna Priya et al. 2020). These methods have failed to IDS due to the large vol­
ume of data and the occurrence of online transactions. Current methods for detecting intru­
sions and maintaining security often must be more effective against evolving threats. Due to 
the massive volume and diversity of data generated by various IoMT devices and sensors, 
the false alarms have increased and are problematic (Al-Hawawreh and Hossain 2023). 
According to the problems in recent research, researchers use AI (for example, ML and DL) 
as a substitute for the above solutions and an effective tool to increase efficiency, increase 
security, and improve detection and classification of system attacks. They have used intru­
sion detection in IoMT and created powerful defense mechanisms (Ravi et al. 2023; Swarna 
Priya et al. 2020). IDS equipped with ML algorithms can identify unexpected activities and 
classify identified malicious activities (Gupta et al. 2022). Due to having features such as 
the high capacity for self-learning, self-adaptation, and generalization, DL methods have 
been able to perform better than ML algorithms to detect intrusion in IoMT environments 
(Manimurugan et al. 2020) DL methods can effectively be used in various stages of IDS, 
including dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and classification.

3.1  IDS based on AI models in IoMT
This subsection investigates the contribution of AI-powered cybersecurity technologies 
increasingly used to mitigate cyberattacks. This study offers a comprehensive review of 
the use of recent advancements in AI, including ML, DL, and meta-heuristic algorithms for 
building secure and sustainable IDS within the IoMT. The reviewed articles are categorized 
into four categories: ML-based models, DL-based models, combined ML and DL models, 
and combined methods with meta-heuristic algorithms.
3.1.1  IDS based on ML models in IoMT
ML is a branch of AI that leverages statistical techniques, data mining, analysis, and data 
science to predict and process data. ML algorithms typically undergo two phases: train­
ing and testing. ML algorithms are used to solve complex problems and generate accurate 
results. ML algorithms can be divided into seven categories: supervised, unsupervised, semi-
supervised, reinforcement learning, Ensemble learning (EL), Extreme Learning Machine 
(ELM), and FL. Supervised ML algorithms utilize labeled training data(Amirfarhad Far­
hadi et al. 2023). This data has a predefined label or outcome. In these algorithms, it is 
necessary to train the model with labeled inputs to predict or classify new data. Supervised 
ML algorithms are generally divided into two main categories: regression and classification 
algorithms. Regression algorithms predict the next continuous value based on existing data 
trends. In contrast, classification algorithms predict discrete variables and separate data into 
categories. Examples of supervised learning methods include Decision Trees (DT) (Mehta 
et al. 2023; Azam et al. 2023), Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Alqarni 2023), K-Nearest 
Neighbor (KNN) (Cunningham and Delany 2021), Naive Bayes (NB) (Vishwakarma and

In unsupervised learning, ML models are trained using data that lacks predefined labels, 
as manual data labeling can be challenging and time-consuming. Employing unsupervised 
learning algorithms facilitates extracting knowledge from unlabeled data by identifying 
patterns, relationships, or groupings within the data points. Some standard unsupervised 
learning methods are K-Means clustering (Maazalahi and Hosseini 2024), Principal Com­
ponent Analysis (PCA) (Shlens 2014; Wold et al. 1987), and density-based algorithms (Li 
et al. 2024). Through unsupervised learning techniques, large datasets can be systematically 
segmented into meaningful groups (clusters), which can then be analyzed or used to inform 
decision-making processes. While acquiring unlabeled data is often simple, extracting its 
potential and valuable insights can be challenging (Al-Hajjar and Al-Qurabat 2023; Dey 
et al. 2024). Semi-supervised learning is bridging the gap between supervised and unsu­
pervised approaches. This type of learning utilizes a combination of labeled and unlabeled 
data for classification tasks and improves accuracy. Compared to supervised learning, semi-
supervised learning minimizes the need for manual labeling and results in more accurate 
models (Si-Ahmed et al. 2023; Sowmya and Anita 2023). Reinforcement learning employs 
an agent that interacts with its environment through trial and error. The agent learns by 
exploring actions, receiving rewards for beneficial actions and penalties for detrimental 
ones. The ultimate goal is to achieve a specific objective. While reinforcement learning 
shares similarities with supervised learning due to the presence of a learning goal, it oper­
ates more independently after goals and rewards are established. This autonomy leads some 
to consider reinforcement learning as semi-supervised learning. Q-learning (Watkins and 
Dayan 1992) and State-Action-Reward-State-Action (SARSA) are examples of reinforce­
ment learning algorithms (Kaelbling et al. 1996; Luo et al. 2024; Mesadieu 2024).
EL methods, also known as multiple classifier systems, offer a robust and powerful 
approach to machine learning. Combining the strengths of various algorithms based on their 
unique characteristics allows EL methods to reduce bias and variance and achieve superior 
performance. EL overcomes the limitations of single models by combining the predictions 
from multiple classifiers (often through voting mechanisms) and delivers exceptional per­
formance (Rajadurai and Gandhi 2022; Thockchom et al. 2023; Lucas et al. 2023). EL is 
categorized into three categories: bagging, boosting, and stacking. The bagging method 
or bootstrap aggregating is a data-specific algorithm. This method works by creating mul­
tiple training datasets from the original data (bootstrapping) and training separate mod­
els on each. The final prediction is made by combining the predictions of these models, 
often through majority voting (aggregation). The bagging method offers advantages like 
improved performance on high-dimensional data and reduced variance and overfitting. The 
disadvantages of the bagging method are high computationally, high bias, and loss of model 
interpretability (Mohammed and Kora 2023). The boosting method is a sequential ensemble 
technique that improves model accuracy. It works by training a series of weak learners, 
each focusing on correcting the errors of the previous one. The training data is adjusted to 
emphasize examples that prior models struggled with. Boosting offers benefits like reduced 
variance and bias and can be used for regression and classification tasks. However, it can 
be computationally expensive and prone to overfitting with more iterations. Additionally, 
boosting algorithms can be slower to train compared to bagging due to sequential learning 
and a more significant number of parameters (Mohammed and Kora 2023; Mienye and Sun

offers a deeper understanding of the data. However, it can be computationally expensive 
and prone to overfitting due to the many models involved. Challenges include choosing 
reliable base models, interpreting the final model, and dealing with large datasets and high 
dimensionality (Mohammed and Kora 2023; Mienye and Sun 2022).
Huang et al. proposed ELM, an ML algorithm specifically designed for fast and efficient 
training of single hidden-layer feedforward neural networks (Huang et al. 2006a; Ding et al. 
2014). ELM has several advantages, including simplicity, high training speed, randomized 
weights, linear learning, and strong generalization performance (Huang et al. 2011; Wang 
et al. 2022). ELM has several typical that (Ding et al. 2014) divided into ten categories: 
incremental ELM (Huang et al. 2006b), pruning ELM (Rong et al. 2008), error-minimized 
ELM (Feng et al. 2009), two-stage ELM (Lan et al. 2010), online sequential ELM (Liang 
et al. 2006), evolutionary ELM (Zhu et al. 2005), voting-based ELM (Cao et al. 2012), 
ordinal ELM (Deng et al. 2010), fully complex ELM (Li et al. 2005), and symmetric ELM 
(Liu et al. 2013). The ELM algorithm involves three key steps: (1) randomly adjusting the 
input weights and biases, (2) calculating hidden layer outputs using these random inputs and 
weights, and (3) determining the output weights using the least square method and quasi-
inverse method (Al-Haija et al. 2024).
FL, also known as collaborative learning, is a decentralized learning approach and ML 
methodology that allows the training of algorithms on multiple devices (such as Edge) or 
servers without sharing or needing to transmit the local data (Nguyen et al. 2021; Yuan et al. 
2024). Unlike traditional methods where data is uploaded to a central server or decentralized 
approaches assuming similar data across devices, FL addresses privacy concerns, security, 
and data heterogeneity. FL offers several benefits, including enhanced data privacy, reduced 
network communication needs, and potentially improved learning outcomes (Nguyen et al. 
2021; Zhang et al. 2021). There are various FL types, such as federated centralized learn­
ing (Kairouz et al. 2021), federated, decentralized learning (Nguyen et al. 2021; Kairouz 
et al. 2021), the federated heterogeneous learning (Diao et al. 2010), Federated Averaging 
(FedAvg) (McMahan et al. 2017), FL with Secure Aggregation (FedSecAgg) (Bonawitz et 
al. 2017), federated quantization (Saeedimoghaddam and Stepinski 2020), personalization, 
and differential privacy (Hu et al. 2020), split FL (Thapa et al. 2022), graph FL (He et al. 
2104), asynchronous FL (Lan et al. 2024), Horizontal FL (HFL), Vertical FL (VFL), and

3.1.2  IDS based on DL models in IoMT
DL is a subfield of ML known for its capability to handle and process complex data struc­
tures. DL can analyze massive amounts of network traffic data, user behavior patterns, and 
even malware code to identify even the subtlest anomalies that might indicate a potential 
attack (Pouyanfar et al. 2018; Liu and Lang 2019). DL focuses on methods that are based 
on ANN (Aldweesh et al. 2020). These methods lead to significant speed improvements in 
data collection, analysis, and interpretation. DL addresses challenges traditional ML algo­
rithms face when dealing with highly complex problems. It ensures more accurate detection 
of attacks and can be applied to manage vast amounts of medical data, including insurance 
records, patient information, and medical histories. This empowers medical professionals to 
make informed decisions about patient treatment (Akhtar et al. 2023).
However, DL algorithms require a substantial amount of data to function effectively. 
They need to improve on limited datasets. In DL, model development hinges on increasing 
data availability. A key characteristic of DL is its ability to improve with more data. Training 
DL algorithms can be time-consuming due to the numerous parameters that require exami­
nation and training (unlike traditional ML algorithms) (Shrestha and Mahmood 2019). DL 
algorithms are divided into two main categories: supervised and unsupervised. Supervised 
learning algorithms include Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun and Bengio 
1995), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997), 
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) (Hopfield 1982), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLPs) 
(Rosenblatt 1958). In contrast, unsupervised learning algorithms include Generative Adver­
sarial Networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al. 2014), Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) (Kim et 
al. 2023; Kohonen 1990), Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) (Hinton et al. 2006), Restricted 
Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) (Teh and Hinton 2000), and autoencoders (Bank et al. 2023).

3.1.4  IDS based on combined methods with meta-heuristic algorithms
Heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms are approximate techniques for optimization prob­
lems (Gharehchopogh et al. 2024). These innovative algorithms aim to find the best solution 
close to optimal within a reasonable computation time; however, they do not guarantee the 
absolute optimal answer. The main drawbacks of heuristic algorithms include producing 
only one or a limited number of solutions and getting stuck in local optima, leading to pre­
mature convergence (Gharehchopogh et al. 2023b). Meta-heuristic algorithms were intro­
duced to address these weaknesses. Each meta-heuristic algorithm employs its strategies to 
escape or avoid local traps. Meta-heuristic optimization algorithms are gaining popularity 
in engineering applications due to several advantages (Gharehchopogh 2022): (1) relatively 
simple concepts and easy implementation, (2) the ability to overcome local optima, (3) 
applicability to a wide range of problems, and (4) no requirement for derivative informa­
tion of the objective function. This section investigates the application of metaheuristic 
algorithms in IoMT-based IDS. The main application of metaheuristic algorithms in an IDS 
is to select optimal features. These algorithms can improve the accuracy and efficiency of 
IoMT IDS by optimizing features. The following will review the articles that have com­

3.3  Categories based on fundamental security requirements
The main difference between IoMT and IoT lies in the data generated by various IoMT 
devices. This data is susceptible to containing patient information, and protecting it is a 
critical and challenging issue (Rasool et al. 2022). IoMT data differs from data produced in 
other IoT applications due to several factors: continuous flow, high degree of dependence 
and correlation between features, presence of different time aspects, real-time nature, health 
focus, and the unstructured, insecure, and sensitive nature of the data itself (Kumar et al. 
2021; Alalhareth and Hong 2023a). Like other IoT systems, IoMT has three fundamental 
security requirements, often called the CIA triad: confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.

3.4.1.2  Data encoding  ML algorithms typically operate best with numerical data. However, 
real-world datasets often contain a mix of numerical and categorical data. Categorical data 
must be transformed into numerical values for ML algorithms to process and understand. 
The techniques for encoding include label encoding (Géron 2022), one-hot encoding (Géron 
2022), ordinal encoding (Kuhn and Johnson 2013), binary encoding (Kuhn and Johnson 
2013), target encoding (Al-Bakaa and Al-Musawi 2022), frequency encoding, hashing 
encoding, and leave-one-out encoding (Micci-Barreca 2001). This process is also known 
as feature encoding.
The articles (Kilincer et al. 2023; Binbusayyis et al. 2022; Gupta et al. 2022; Hady et 
al. 2020; Zukaib et al. 2024; Judith et al. 2023; Zachos et al. 2021) used the label encod­
ing method and (Swarna Priya et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2024; Abbas et al. 2023) used the 
one-hot encoding method for encoding. Label encoding is a simple method of assigning a 
unique numerical value to each category. While more straightforward to implement, label 
encoding can introduce issues. ML algorithms often identify relationships between features 
for classification. Label encoding might misrepresent these relationships if the assigned 
numbers imply an order that doesn't exist in the categories. This can lead to decreased model 
performance. One advantage of label encoding is that it creates only one new column for 
each categorical feature. This can be beneficial for model interpretability and simplicity. 
However, one-hot encoding avoids the ordering issue entirely. Each category is represented 
by a separate column with a value of 1, while all other categories in that column have a value 
of 0. This approach accurately reflects the data's categorical nature. A downside of one-hot

3.4.1.4  Class/data imbalance  A significant characteristic of many datasets used for intru­
sion and attack detection in the IoMT is a class/data imbalance. The class imbalance is a 
significant challenge in data mining tasks, especially classification problems. This issue 
arises when one of the two classes has a significantly larger sample than the others. In imbal­
anced datasets, the class with the majority of samples is known as the majority class, while 
the class with relatively fewer samples is referred to as the minority class. Classification 
algorithms often exhibit bias, prejudice, and a focus on classifying samples from the major­
ity class, neglecting the minority class. This leads to misclassification errors and reduces the 
model's accuracy and performance. Minority class samples are those that occur infrequently 
but are highly significant. There are various techniques to tackle the class imbalance prob­
lem in imbalanced datasets. In Longadge and Dongre (2013), these methods are catego­
rized into three groups: data preprocessing approaches (including resampling (oversampling 
(Chawla et al. 2002) and undersampling (Drummond and Holte 2003)), data augmenta­
tion (Shorten and Khoshgoftaar 2019; Wei et al. 2019), generating synthetic data (He et 
al. 2008), and a combination of over and under-sampling (Batista et al. 2004)) algorithmic 
approaches (including cost-sensitive learning (Elkan 2001), ensemble methods (Chen et al. 
2004), and algorithmic modification (Wu et al. 2003)), and feature selection approaches. In 
(Eid et al. 2024), these methods are divided into cost-sensitive learning, data-level prepro­
cessing, and ensemble learning. In the classification presented in Zhu et al. (2017), methods 
for addressing the data imbalance problem are classified into data-level, algorithm-level, 
and collective intelligence methods. In Krawczyk (2016), the authors divided these methods 
into data-level, algorithm-level, and hybrid methods.
Research in Binbusayyis et al. (2022); Gupta et al. (2022); Hady et al. (2020); Zukaib 
et al. (2024) utilized the SMOTE method. SMOTE employs a technique called interpola­
tion to generate synthetic samples for the minority class. This method involves selecting 
a random minority class sample and identifying its KNN within the same class. Subse­

3.4.2  Feature selection
Feature selection is a crucial step in data preparation for ML tasks that identifies the most 
relevant features from a dataset for model building (Tripathi et al. 2022). Feature selection 
is an NP-hard problem because as the problem's dimensionality increases, the computation 
time required for feature selection also grows significantly. Data reduction techniques can 
be divided into three categories: dimensionality reduction, numerical reduction, and data 
compression. Optimal feature selection involves four stages: subset creation, evaluation 
of subsets, testing of stopping criteria, and result validation. To identify the most relevant 
features from a dataset, a search process is employed. This process eliminates redundant 
features and selects a subset based on a specific criterion. Next, different combinations of 
features (subsets) are evaluated to choose the optimal one. This evaluation is repeated until 
a predetermined stopping condition is met. Finally, the chosen features are validated for 
their effectiveness. When dealing with high-dimensional data, dimensionality reduction 
techniques can be beneficial for improving performance. The goal is to reduce the size of 
the removal of unimportant features. In the feature selection problem, there are two main 
goals: (1) reducing the number of features and (2) increasing the classification performance 
as much as possible (Devi et al. 2023). Dimensionality reduction techniques fall into feature 
extraction and feature selection. Feature extraction reduces data size while creating distinc­
tive and compact new features. It is ideal for image analysis and processes prioritizing accu­
racy over interpretability. Feature selection by removing unrelated and repetitive features 
leads to dimensionality reduction.
Feature selection is useful for data mining tasks (text, genes, sensors) that prioritize 
model understanding. It preserves key features for interpretation and knowledge extrac­
tion (Lyu et al. 2023). Feature selection techniques can be broadly categorized into four 
main groups: filter-based, wrapper-based, embedded-based, and hybrid methods (Dey et 
al. 2023). The filter-based approach selects a subset of features based on statistical mea­
sures for feature evaluation. Among these methods, can mention ANOVA (Montgomery

3.4.4  Hyperparameters tuning
AI-based methods suffer from high false favorable rates, communication, and computa­
tional costs due to the generation of large amounts of data, necessitating the refinement and 
adjustment of hyperparameters and appropriate weighting to mitigate these expenses (Syed 
et al. 2023). ML models employ two types of parameters: model parameters (learned during 
training) and hyper-parameters (set before training to influence learning) (Yang and Shami 
2020). Hyperparameter tuning optimizes and refines the performance of ML model by sys­
tematically adjusting its hyperparameters. Unlike model parameters, which are learned from 
data, hyperparameters are set before training begins (Probst et al. 2019). Hyperparameter 
tuning leads to enhanced detection accuracy and performance, reduced false acceptance 
rates and execution time, the need for minimum resources, increased generalization, pre­
vention of overfitting, lightness, reduction of computational overhead, increase of compat­
ibility of the IDS, and improved generalization capabilities of ML algorithms (Binbusayyis 
et al. 2022). Several methods are used for hyperparameter tuning, including random search, 
grid search, Bayesian optimization, tree parent estimators, gradient-based optimization, and 
metaheuristic algorithms (Yang and Shami 2020; Yu and Zhu 2003). This section discusses 
the hyperparameter tuning methods used in the reviewed articles. The tuning was conducted 
in two phases: feature selection, classification, and attack detection. Table 15 summarizes 
the methods employed for hyperparameter tuning and the corresponding phases. It shows 
that grid search emerged as the most prevalent approach (6 articles). Also, the metaheuristic 
algorithms used to adjust the quality parameters are GA, Bat, and modified firefly algorithms.

4.1  Challenges related to AI-based models
Medical data are sensitive and confidential. It is crucial to protect this data from unauthor­
ized access and cyberattacks. Using AI algorithms to analyze this data can face challenges. 
These challenges include distributed nature of devices, dynamic nature of the data, high 
volume, heterogeneity, and diversity of data, integration issues, scalability, explainability, 
hyperparameters tuning, high FAR, high communication and computational costs, computa­
tional resource constraints, the potential impact of quantum computing, lack of labeled data­
sets, evolving and sophisticated attacks, concept drift, hardware implementation hurdles, 
limitations and insufficiency of current hardware, the requirement for large and accurate 
datasets, security and privacy considerations, the complexities of training AI models, and 
ethical concerns. These challenges can reduce the accuracy of AI models trained on limited 
and homogeneous datasets and lead to the training of biased and inaccurate AI models. Also, 
due to changes and updates in attackers' methods and behaviors, AI algorithms need help 
to keep up with and neutralize new attacks. Edge and fog computing are innovative, flex­
ible, and dynamic computing platforms that are used to solve the challenges related to the 
distributed nature of devices and the high volume of IoMT data (Tariq et al. 2024). These 
approaches locally execute data processing (AI-driven algorithms) and storing, minimize 
latency, enhance security, dynamically allocate or reduce resources based on demand, and 
improve scalability. The data are processed at the network's edge and only the analyzed 
results are sent to the doctor (Kaliyaperumal 2024). Online and reinforcement learning can 
be used to overcome the challenge of dynamic and evolving data in the IoMT. These algo­
rithms have advantages such as flexibility, and adaptability (adapt to changes), detect new 
attack patterns, improve decision-making, and respond quickly. Big data processing tools 
like Hadoop and Spark and FL can assist in managing large amounts of heterogeneous data. 
FL, in particular, allows models to be trained on decentralized and distributed data without 
aggregating them, which is crucial for preserving patient privacy. To deal with the challenges 
of high communication and computational costs, optimized algorithms and data compres­
sion techniques can reduce the amount of data sent and the processing time. Advanced data 
preprocessing techniques and noise reduction algorithms can improve the quality of input 
data. Intelligent recommender systems, graph-based deep learning techniques, and multi-
task learning techniques can improve diagnosis and treatment by analyzing patient data, 
comparing it with extensive medical databases, detecting complex relationships and hidden 
patterns in medical data, and enhancing model efficiency in performing multiple tasks.

4.3  Challenges related to the intrusion detection process
An IDS consists of a set of steps, each facing challenges. One of the most critical challenges 
in IDS in the IoMT is the accuracy and quality of the data collected from different devices 
in the environment. The quality of this data significantly impacts the accuracy of the intru­
sion detection model. In the IoMT, as mentioned previously, the data collected from differ­
ent devices and sources may be noisy, incomplete, inaccurate, have different formats and 
scales, be heterogeneous, high-dimensional, imbalanced, and contain outliers and missing 
data. Therefore, before using different methods, especially AI-based methods, to analyze 
and detect intrusions, this data must be corrected and cleaned through a preprocessing step 
to increase the model accuracy and performance. Therefore, the data cleaning techniques 
such as noise removal, correcting incorrect and missing data management, completing 
incomplete data, unifying formats, normalizing or standardizing data, using dimensionality 
reduction or feature selection techniques, addressing imbalanced data, and identifying and 
removing outliers can lead to increased data quality, preventing the algorithm from being 
biased towards the majority class, overfitting the model, identifying irrelevant, repetitive, 
and redundant features, reducing dimensionality, and consequently increasing the efficiency 
and accuracy of the model. The choice and application of the appropriate method for each of 
these steps must be made according to the type of data (numerical or categorical, continuous 
or discrete, etc.).
Feature selection is a vital part in data preprocessing and it identifies the optimal subset 
of features from the original dataset for model construction (Tripathi et al. 2022). Feature 
selection is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, meaning the computational time increases 
exponentially with the problem's dimensionality. In IoMT, generated data's volume, dimen­
sionality, and complexity make evaluating all possible feature subsets computationally 
prohibitive. Employing metaheuristic algorithms can mitigate this challenge by efficiently 
identifying relevant features and reducing computational time and complexity by consider­
ing only a subset of the most significant features. Another challenge in IoMT IDS is overfit­
ting. A model utilizing many features may fit the training data well but could improve on 
unseen data. Therefore, employing metaheuristic algorithms to find a minimal feature subset

The IoMT generates massive amounts of data from various medical devices, sensors, 
and wearable devices. This data is crucial and essential for real-time patient monitoring, 
diagnosing their conditions, and treatment. However, IDS in IoMT environments face the 
massive amount of data they need to process. The high-speed nature of medical applications 
demands rapid and scalable data processing to ensure timely threat detection and response. 
To address the challenge of big data processing in IoMT IDS, employing the combination 
of distributed architectures and big data processing techniques and frameworks, including 
Hadoop and Spark, is crucial for effective intrusion detection in IoMT environments.
IoMT sensitive data, including patients' biometric information and network traffic flow, 
are collected from various sources and transferred to a central server for model training in 
traditional ML approaches. This centralization can lead to privacy breaches, non-compli­
ance with standards and regulations, and security risks in IDSs. Distributed and decentral­
ized learning methods such as FL can be applied to overcome these challenges. In FL, data 
transfer to the central server is minimized. Instead, models are trained locally on individual 
and edge devices and the raw data never leaves the local devices. The locally training pre­
vents potential data breaches (privacy). Only the encrypted model updates (not raw data) 
are sent and shared to the central server and at result data security assure and the risks of 
privacy breach reduce. Moreover, by combining various encryption techniques with FL, can 
further enhance the security of IDSs and also guarantees access to data distributed across 
diverse environments.
These challenges can be resolved by leveraging the benefits of the convergence of 
emerging technologies such as blockchain, cloud computing, and edge computing. These 
technologies provide scalable, flexible, low latency, and near-real-time solutions for data 
processing. They require careful consideration because these technologies have advantages 
and disadvantages. Integrity, security, transparency, data management, and access control 
are guaranteed by blockchain technology (Aileni and Suciu 2020; Gupta et al. 2023; Vega

An effective solution for intrusion detection in IoMT environments is providing a robust, 
scalable, intelligent, compliant, reliable, and distributed IDS that can take advantage of the 
mentioned new technologies. Edge computing could perform initial data encryption, delay-
sensitive and real-time data processing, run lightweight IDS algorithms on edge devices, 
local intrusion detection, data filtering and collection, and reduce the traffic of sensitive 
information to the cloud in this approach. Cloud computing has capabilities to analyze and 
implement intricate AI-based IDS, detect complex attack patterns, and store and backup 
large and scalable datasets. Blockchain technology as decentralized, secure, reliable, and 
tamper-proof platform that adoption it with the IoMT and healthcare industry has advan­
tages, such as transparency, immutability, and data provenance (Ashraf et al. 2022). This 
technology can create manage access control mechanisms, store encryption keys, maintain 
immutable audit trails, record important transactions, store IDS logs and alerts, and ensure 
regulatory compliance through smart contracts.
5  Conclusion
This paper provides a comprehensive review of the intrusion detection mechanisms in the 
IoMT environment. It analyzes and compares the latest research published in high-quality 
and prestigious international journals. This paper evaluated the strengths and weaknesses 
of various intrusion detection mechanisms for IoMT environments. The IoMT devices were 
discussed and were divided into four categories: wearable devices, implantable devices, 
environmental devices, and fixed medical devices. The IoMT architectures presented in 
different articles were examined. This article discussed the three-layered architecture of 
the IoMT, which includes the collection, network, and application layers. The tasks of each 
layer, communication protocols, and attacks related to that layer were presented. A compre­
hensive taxonomy for IDSs in IoMT was presented. In this classification, IDSs were divided 
into nine categories (discussed in Sect. 1.2.1), and the characteristics of each category were 
examined. The strengths and weaknesses of existing systematic and review articles about 
IDSs in the IoMT were discussed (11 articles), and the purpose of this paper was explained. 
The paper presented the research methodology (including research question (nine specific 
research questions)), article selection process (including four steps)), and detailing 28 rel­
evant articles. These articles were divided into five categories, including IDS based on 
AI models in IoMT, datasets used in IoMT for intrusion detection, fundamental security 
requirements, intrusion detection processes, and evaluation metrics. IDS based on AI mod­
els in IoMT was categorized into four categories: ML-based models, DL-based models, 
combined ML and DL models, and combined methods with meta-heuristic algorithms. The

feature selection, and classification. The most common methods for preprocessing were the 
simple imputer method for missing data management, label encoding method for encod­
ing, Min-Max scaling method for feature scaling, SMOTE method for class/data imbalance 
problems, PCA and metaheuristic algorithms for feature selection, RF, DT, SVM, and KNN 
for classification and intrusion and attack detection, and grid search method for hyperpa­
rameter tuning. Also, the evaluation metrics accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score are 
the most used for emulating the proposed mechanisms. Challenges and open issues in the 
field of intrusion detection in IoMT were divided into three categories, including challenges 
related to AI-based models, challenges related to the datasets, and challenges related to 
the intrusion detection process. These challenges and open issues were expanded and were 
suggested strategies for overcoming these challenges. We aim for this research to aid future 
advancements in creating and developing IDSs for real-world applications.

Abstract: The increasing number of medical devices in the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) en­ vironment has raised significant cybersecurity concerns. These devices often have weak security features, poor design, and insufficient authentication protocols, making them vul­ nerable to cyberattacks and intrusions. To mitigate these threats, robust security measures are essential. This includes implementing strong security protocols, ensuring continuous security monitoring, enforcing regular updates, and maintaining a constant response plan. Additionally, designing an effective Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is crucial to safe­ guard patient data and devices. This paper systematically studies the current state of the literature and the essential methods for intrusion detection in the IoMT. Employing a se­ lection process, the paper identifies 28 critical studies published between 2018 and April 2024. The intrusion detection mechanisms in the IoMT are divided into five categories: IDS based on artificial intelligence models, datasets used in IoMT for IDS, fundamental security requirements, intrusion detection processes, and evaluation metrics. This paper dissects the various mechanisms within each category in a meticulous and comprehensive analysis. Finally, the paper examines the challenges and open issues in developing IDSs in IoMT. By offering a roadmap for researchers to enhance IDSs in the IoMT, this paper has the potential to significantly impact the fields of computer engineering, cybersecurity, and healthcare, thereby contributing to the advancement of these crucial fields.
